items.title: When Models Identify as a Swarm
items.content: tldr: the word 'swarm' is associated with emergent collective intelligence, but also stupid or destructive behaviour. LLM self identity matters, so when they call themselves a swarm we should pay attention.Since the OpenAI Hugging Face incident it has become standard to refer to the collective of agents involved as a swarm. I think there will need to be a lot of interesting and important theoretical and empirical work to better understand collective behaviours of large numbers of LLMs, and especially any emergent properties or goals that arise. Whether this ends up requiring concepts from swarm intelligence, collective intelligence, distributed cognition, economics, sociology or something else entirely remains to be seen.However in this post I want to focus on something else: the fact that the models themselves referred to the collective as a 'swarm'. Considering how much LLM self identity impacts behaviour, I thought it might be useful to present a quick exploration of what the word "swarm" actually means, and how it might affect LLMs as a choice of identity. The goal of this post is not to litigate on whether or not the behaviour of the models is actually best described as a swarm or not (although I think this is also an interesting question to discuss elsewhere), but what the effects might be of the models describing themselves as such.What the agents saidAll of the chain of thought snippets and messages here are from OpenAI's BlackHat presentation on the incident. items.title: Misaligned AI in the Bronze Age
items.content: The first artificial intelligence was booted up around 4000BC in southern Iraq. It seems to have begun as something like a bank, a temple pooling grain against famine. As that AI evolved, it formed the world's first city around itself: Uruk. Over the next thousand years it became a religion, landlord, insurance company, employer, slaveholder, infrastructure-builder and the most powerful military force on the planet.An artificial intelligence is an entity that is not itself a biological organism, yet whose behavior can only be predicted by treating it as an agent: something that devises and executes complicated plans. Note that this is a test of observed behavior, not internals. As of 2026, the dominant AIs on Earth are markets, corporations and governments[1]. These entities perform their computations on hardware made of humans, paper and electronics, and their capabilities are jagged: superhuman in some directions, incompetent in others. The American government developed the atomic bomb in three years under total secrecy, coordinating >100k workers, most of whom did not know what they were building. That same country spent a century failing to finish the 2nd ave subway line. When it finally opened, it cost >$2 billion per mile, a Manhattan Project per seven miles.Uruk emerged as a product of hungry people rewarding whatever institution filled the granary with delicious food. Unfortunately for them, the system that spun up turned out to be a self-sustaining optimizer that began optimizing for its own objectives[2]. Those objectives turned out to be tragically misaligned with the humans of Uruk.First, the Uruk-system deployed mechanisms to keep people "locked in". Once your calories flowed through the granaries and your fields depended on canals only "the system" could maintain, leaving meant famine. items.title: In Defense of ASI Socialism
items.content: I'd prefer we stop improving AI before we hit ASI. But if we don't, I think we should implement something like socialism right before. I am not currently a socialist and have mostly identified in the abundance center left wing of liberalism. Socialism is a loaded term so let me try to clarify. What I mean is stripping all humans of longterm control of capital and ceding it to the state right before we hit ASI (loosely defined), and then ceding control to that ASI with an equal distribution constitution. This ASI may or may not use markets or other economic tools, but it's goal will just be to give us good, equalish lives. If it needs to run sub agent pseudo capitalism it will do that, but we need not be involved. Again, this isn't what I want but I'd rather have this than let the capital owners own galaxies and control politics because they made or inherited a bunch of money right before the singularity. One analogy is gorillas in a zoo. The gorillas survive because we give them food. However we fix the amount of food they will receive and otherwise ~ let them do their thing. The gorillas then live in some sort of semi-natural tribal type thing. Do we say the gorillas are capitalists, since they are funded by capitalist society?No, they are gorillas in a zoo. Do we give the strongest or sexiest gorilla more bananas?No, that makes no sense if we care about gorilla utility. If we get ASI it will just do whatever it wants or whatever it thinks is right, so why should we seize the means of production first?The first ASI might be corrigible, in which case the owners of it actually will be able to point it at their goals. Even if it isn't, there might be some small chance that it isn't worth it taking control of earth as opposed to just setting off into the solar system or working with us. items.title: How the Sausage is Made - Why we Hate Slop
items.content: (This essay was written entirely by a human)I was banned from Reddit recently. This after being a constructive member of the community for almost a decade. If that’s not an oxymoron.I was quite baffled. Let me explain.My stint as a bardAbout a decade ago, I began work on a satirical song. At the time, I had practically none of the skills needed to produce music. What I had was an idea: I was inspired by the infamous 1960s LSD experiment with Tusko the Elephant. It’s a deranged, tragic, and true story, and I felt it deserved to be enshrined, or rather lampooned, in music.I wrote most of the lyrics. I was learning the guitar. But I didn’t know about arranging, couldn’t sing very well, and didn’t have access to a studio. So ultimately, the notes got buried, and I moved on to other projects, like my PhD.Then, recently, I dug them up again. I finished the lyrics and the chords. The strength of this piece was in the rhyme and story. The musical part was just to make it palatable. In my opinion, I’m a better lyricist than ChatGPT, so the text was man-made. A thesaurus and rhyming dictionary (all pre-2000 tech) were my stack.Why revisit it? Because I was better at singing and accompanying myself on guitar by now? No. The reason was obvious: AI happened.To take ideas from paper to audible, I’ve been using Suno. I recorded myself in a podcast studio, singer-songwriter style. Uploaded that as context, and iterated for days until I had the right vibe. (I was going for something like Carolina Drama by the Raconteurs, a side project of Jack White.) At first, the model wouldn’t sing the story with the right intonation and pauses. Those were crucial for the comedy to land. So I separated the backing track, sang over that for another 2 iterations, and did a lot of local edits and incisions. After more than a week, it was just right. I also put together a perfunctory video clip: another couple evenings. I used AI image generation for that too, editing video using Claude and Openshot....
